pos: n. pl. (the resolutions of the Commission of the Scottish General Assembly, 1650–51, admitting former Engagers to the defence of the kingdom)
etymology: public, from Latin publicus, of the people; resolution, from Latin resolutio, a loosening, a determination.
biblical_def: The Public Resolutions were the answers given by the Commission of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, in December 1650 and again in 1651, to a question put by the Committee of Estates after Cromwell had destroyed the Scottish army at Dunbar: whether men excluded from public trust by the Act of Classes — the Engagers of 1648 and the followers of Montrose — might now be employed in the defence of the kingdom. The Commission answered that in such extremity they might. The reasoning was that the invasion threatened the very existence of the covenanted nation, that necessity permitted the use of any hand that would fight, and that the alternative was conquest. The answer split the Church of Scotland in two. Those who accepted it were the Resolutioners; those who protested against it were the Protesters, and the breach was never healed before the Restoration swept both away. The question was not whether the men were needed but whether a covenanted church may employ those it has judged unfit. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines necessity as that which makes an act unavoidable, and a resolution as a formal determination of an assembly.
webster_full: NECES'SITY, n. That which makes an act or event unavoidable; compulsion; irresistible force.
RESOLU'TION, n. A formal determination of a public body or assembly; a fixed purpose.
EN'GAGER, n. One who engages or binds himself; in Scottish history, a subscriber of the Engagement of 1648.
EXTREM'ITY, n. The utmost point; the highest degree; the most pressing distress.
scriptures: Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Jdg 7:2
And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.
Jdg 7:3

Now therefore go to, proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand.

And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.
corruption_summary: The 1650 answer on employing excluded men, which split the Church of Scotland.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument from necessity that carried the Public Resolutions is perpetually available and perpetually dangerous. It is the reasoning by which churches in every generation suspend their own standards for an emergency: the cause is just, the danger is real, the help is needed, and the rule can be kept again afterwards. There was no afterwards. Within a decade the men whom the Resolutions readmitted, or men of their party, were the government that drove the covenanted ministers out of their parishes.

The principle to recover is that God's cause is not advanced by numbers and is not lost for want of them, which is the whole lesson of Gideon's army: “The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands” (Jdg 7:2). Jonathan states the same from the other side: “for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” (1Sa 14:6).

pos: n. pl. (the party in the Church of Scotland that protested against the Public Resolutions of 1650–51)
etymology: protest, from Latin protestari, to declare publicly, bear witness before; the party's name is taken from the formal protestations it entered.
biblical_def: The Scottish Protesters were the minority of ministers and elders who entered formal protestations against the Public Resolutions and against the Assembly of 1651 that approved them. Their leaders were Samuel Rutherford, James Guthrie, Patrick Gillespie, Archibald Johnston of Wariston and Andrew Cant, with the younger ministers of the west and north largely with them. Their case was simple and hard: the Church had solemnly judged the Engagers unfit for public trust on the ground of the Covenant, and no national emergency entitled it to unsay that judgment; to call back the men who had broken the Covenant in order to defend the covenanted kingdom was to destroy the thing being defended. They lost the vote, were outvoted in every court, and were vindicated by what followed: when Charles II returned in 1660, the Protesters were the men who would not conform, and the Covenanting remnant of the killing times came from their line. “Who will rise up for me against the evildoers?” (Psa 94:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to protest as to make a solemn declaration against something, and to reprove as to blame, to censure to the face.
webster_full: PROTEST', v. To make a solemn declaration, expressive of opposition; to declare against.
REPROVE', v. To blame; to censure to the face; to charge with a fault; to chide.
PROTESTA'TION, n. A solemn declaration of a fact, opinion or resolution; a solemn declaration against.
REM'NANT, n. That which is left; residue; the small surviving part.
scriptures: Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? or who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity?

And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD.
Jdg 5:23
Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
Eph 5:11
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
corruption_summary: The minority who protested the Resolutions and became the Covenanting remnant.
corruption_paragraphs: The Protesters are regularly presented, and were presented in their own day, as rigid men who preferred a clean conscience to a surviving nation — sectaries who divided the church in the hour of invasion. The charge has to be weighed against the sequel. The Resolutioners' necessity did not save Scotland from Cromwell; the Protesters' principle was what stood when Charles returned, and the ministers who went to the scaffold and the hillside were almost all of their party. Scrupulous men are not always wrong about which concession is fatal.

The principle to recover is that the people of God may not lend their strength to those who hate him, however convenient the alliance: “Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?” (2Ch 19:2). And the duty is not merely abstention but open testimony: “And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11).

pos: n. pl. (the majority party in the Church of Scotland that accepted the Public Resolutions of 1650–51)
etymology: From the Public Resolutions they defended; resolution from Latin resolutio, a determination.
biblical_def: The Resolutioners were the majority of the Church of Scotland's ministers who accepted the Public Resolutions and held the Assemblies of 1651 and after. Their leaders were Robert Douglas, Robert Baillie, David Dickson, Robert Blair and James Sharp, men of real learning and in most cases real piety; they argued that the Covenant bound the nation to defend the king and the kingdom, that the Act of Classes had disarmed Scotland before an invader, and that a church which forbade the use of every imperfect instrument would hand the country to Cromwell. The Protesters answered that this was to trust an arm of flesh. What followed judged between them in a way neither expected: Cromwell won anyway, the Assemblies were dissolved by his soldiers, and at the Restoration the Resolutioner party divided, most of its ministers suffering deprivation in 1662 while their own envoy James Sharp became the archbishop who hunted the rest. “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help” (Isa 31:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expediency as fitness to effect some good end, and an arm of flesh as human strength as distinguished from divine.
webster_full: EXPE'DIENCY, n. Fitness or suitableness to effect some good end; propriety under the circumstances.
ARM, n. Figuratively, power, might; an arm of flesh, human strength or help.
MAJOR'ITY, n. The greater number; more than half of any number.
DEPRIVA'TION, n. The act of depriving; the taking away of a clergyman's preferment.
scriptures: Isa 31:1

Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!

And at that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said unto him, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
corruption_summary: The majority who trusted necessity, and whose own envoy became the persecutor.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a partisan one within Reformed history itself, where the Resolutioners are sometimes written off as the worldly party and the Protesters canonised. The dictionary resists it. Robert Douglas refused a bishopric and was deprived; Robert Blair and David Dickson suffered; most Resolutioner ministers went out in 1662 with the rest. They were wrong on the question of 1651, and the great majority paid for a faithfulness they did not abandon.

The principle to recover is that trust in human means is the besetting sin of a church facing a real danger, and that Scripture names it as sin rather than prudence: “Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God” (2Ch 16:7). The psalm sets the alternative without pretending the chariots are imaginary: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7).

pos: n. (the Act of the Scottish Parliament of January 1649 excluding Engagers and Malignants from public trust)
etymology: class, from Latin classis, a division or rank; the Act sorted the excluded into four classes by degree of guilt.
biblical_def: The Act of Classes was passed by the Scottish Parliament in January 1649, in the brief ascendancy of the strict Covenanting party after the defeat of the Engagement. It excluded from all public office — parliament, council, army, burgh magistracy — everyone who had taken part in the Engagement of 1648 to rescue Charles I on terms the Church judged unlawful, or in Montrose's royalist war, or had otherwise acted against the Covenant; and it sorted them into four classes according to the degree of their offence, with periods of exclusion from one year to life, each requiring evidence of repentance before restoration. It was the high-water mark of the attempt to make a nation's public life answer to a church's judgment of character. It also left Scotland short of experienced officers when Cromwell crossed the border, which is precisely the pressure that produced the Public Resolutions; Parliament repealed it in June 1651. “He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house” (Psa 101:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a class as a rank or order of persons, and to exclude as to thrust out, to hinder from entrance or participation.
webster_full: CLASS, n. An order or rank of persons; a number of persons in society supposed to have the same position.
EXCLUDE', v. To thrust out; to hinder from entrance or admission; to debar from participation.
MALIG'NANT, n. In English and Scottish history, a name given by the Covenanters to the royalists.
REPEAL', v. To recall, as a deed or law; to revoke; to abrogate by authority.
scriptures: He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies shall not tarry in my sight.
Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business;
Ezr 9:2

For they have taken of their daughters for themselves, and for their sons: so that the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands: yea, the hand of the princes and rulers hath been chief in this trespass.

And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD.
corruption_summary: Four classes of exclusion from public trust, passed in 1649 and repealed in 1651.
corruption_paragraphs: The Act of Classes is a standing exhibit for the claim that Reformed political theology ends in theocratic exclusion: a church deciding who may hold office in a commonwealth. The dictionary neither defends the Act as a model nor accepts the caricature. Scotland was a covenanted nation by its own parliament's deed, and the Act applied a condition the nation had sworn to; its practical fault was not that it took public faithfulness seriously but that it bound a kingdom's whole administrative capacity to a classification that could not be revised under pressure except by repeal.

The principle to recover is that public trust is rightly conditioned on character, and that the conditioning is a sound instinct even when a particular statute embodying it is clumsy. David's charter for his own household is exclusionary on exactly that ground: “He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies shall not tarry in my sight” (Psa 101:7). Nehemiah's reform was of the same kind: “Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites” (Neh 13:30).

pos: n. (Patrick Gillespie, 1617–1675, minister of Glasgow, Principal of its university, leading Protester)
etymology: Latin Patricius, a nobleman; Gillespie, from Gaelic gille easbuig, servant of the bishop.
biblical_def: Patrick Gillespie was the younger brother of George Gillespie of the Westminster Assembly and in his own right one of the ablest of the Protesters: minister of Glasgow from 1648, a protester against the Public Resolutions, and from 1653 Principal of the University of Glasgow. He also did the thing that divided his own party. Judging that the Protesters could get from Cromwell's government what they could not get from a royalist one, he went to London in 1654 and obtained from the Protector an ordinance — remembered in Scotland as Gillespie's Charter — which put the planting of parishes and the universities largely in the hands of commissioners favourable to his party. Samuel Rutherford and James Guthrie would have nothing to do with it; many Protesters thought he had taken from an English usurper an authority over the Church of Scotland that belonged to her own assemblies. At the Restoration he lost everything and died in obscurity. “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a charter as a written instrument granting privileges, and an usurper as one who seizes power without right.
webster_full: CHAR'TER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or privilege.
USURP'ER, n. One who seizes or occupies the power or property of another without right.
PRIN'CIPAL, n. The chief or head; the president or governor of a college.
YOKE, v. To couple; to join with another; to enslave.
scriptures: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
And he said unto Jehoshaphat, Wilt thou go with me to battle to Ramothgilead? And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, I am as thou art, my people as thy people, my horses as thy horses.

And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD.
A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring.
corruption_summary: The Protester who took a charter from Cromwell and split his own party.
corruption_paragraphs: Gillespie is the hardest case in the Protester camp, and the dictionary does not resolve it in his favour. He had argued against employing the ungodly in the nation's service and then accepted from an English conqueror a jurisdiction over Scottish parishes that no Scottish assembly had given him. His defence was that the power was being used for faithful men and that the alternative was to leave the planting of churches to worse hands; it is the Resolutioners' argument from necessity in another dress, made by the man who had refused it.

The principle to recover is that an alliance which delivers the church's own government into other hands is not made safe by the good intentions of the man who makes it: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14). Jehoshaphat's answer to Ahab is the model of the cheerful, disastrous alliance — “I am as thou art, my people as thy people, my horses as thy horses” (1Ki 22:4) — and Solomon names what it does to a man's witness: “A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring” (Pro 25:26).

pos: n. (Robert Douglas, 1594–1674, five times Moderator of the Scottish General Assembly, leader of the Resolutioners)
etymology: German Robert, bright fame; Douglas, from Gaelic dubh glas, dark water.
biblical_def: Robert Douglas was the most considerable churchman in Scotland for a generation. Chaplain to the Scots regiments in Germany under Gustavus Adolphus in his youth, minister of Edinburgh from 1641, he was chosen Moderator of the General Assembly five times, preached at the coronation of Charles II at Scone on 1 January 1651 — a sermon of blunt warning to the young king about the Covenant he was swearing — and led the Resolutioner party through the whole controversy. He was wrong about the Public Resolutions, and the dictionary says so in the entry on them. It also records what he did in 1662, when the king he had crowned offered him a bishopric: he refused it, was deprived of his Edinburgh charge, and spent his last twelve years as a nonconforming minister in a country parish, dying in 1674. The man who had argued that the Church might stretch a point for the sake of the king would not stretch one for the king's episcopacy. “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a moderator as the president of a meeting who regulates proceedings, and nonconformity as refusal to unite with an established church.
webster_full: MOD'ERATOR, n. The person who presides over a meeting or assembly to preserve order and regulate proceedings.
NONCONFORM'ITY, n. Neglect or failure of conformity; refusal to unite with an established church.
CORONA'TION, n. The act or solemnity of crowning a sovereign.
CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who performs divine service in an army, a ship or a family.
scriptures: Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.
Ecc 8:2
I counsel thee to keep the king's commandment, and that in regard of the oath of God.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
corruption_summary: The Moderator who crowned Charles II and refused his bishopric.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the tidy partisan reading of 1651 that treats every Resolutioner as a time-server. Douglas crowned a king, warned him to his face in the coronation sermon, led the party that compromised, and then declined the reward when it came and lost his pulpit for it. The historical record will not reduce to two parties of the faithful and the pliable.

The principle to recover is that honour to the magistrate and obedience to God are both commanded and that their order is fixed when they collide. Peter puts the honour unqualified — “Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17) — and he had already settled the precedence before the council: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).

“Mercy and truth preserve the king” (Pro 20:28) — the burden of his coronation sermon.

pos: n. (Andrew Cant, c. 1590–1663, Covenanting preacher of Aberdeen, a Protester)
etymology: Greek Andreas, manly; Cant, a Scottish surname. The English word cant, whining jargon, was wrongly derived from his name by eighteenth-century writers; it is in fact from Latin cantare, to sing.
biblical_def: Andrew Cant was the most formidable Covenanting preacher in the north-east of Scotland. Minister successively at Alford, Newbattle and from 1641 at Aberdeen, he was sent in 1638 with Alexander Henderson and David Dickson to carry the National Covenant to Aberdeen, the most royalist and Episcopal city in the kingdom, and preached it there against the Aberdeen Doctors and a hostile magistracy. He sat in the Westminster Assembly's Scottish delegation's orbit, served as a chaplain in the Covenanting armies, and took the Protesters' side in 1651. His plainness made enemies and made a legend: Samuel Johnson's dictionary and others after him derived the English word cant, for whining sanctimonious talk, from his preaching, which is an etymological slander — the word comes from the Latin for singing — but which shows how a certain kind of preaching was remembered. He was deprived in 1660 and died in 1663. “But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD” (Mic 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cant as a whining, affected or hypocritical manner of speaking, and boldness as freedom from timidity in speaking.
webster_full: CANT, n. A whining, affected or hypocritical manner of speech; the particular jargon of a class or profession.
BOLD'NESS, n. Courage; freedom from timidity in speaking or writing; assurance.
COV'ENANTER, n. One who makes a covenant; in Scotland, an adherent of the National Covenant.
PLAIN'NESS, n. Openness; rough sincerity; freedom from ornament or ambiguity.
scriptures: Mic 3:8
But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD, and of judgment, and of might, to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin.
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Jer 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
corruption_summary: The Aberdeen Covenanter whose name was wrongly made an English word for hypocrisy.
corruption_paragraphs: The false etymology that turned Cant's surname into a word for sanctimonious whining did real work, and the work it did is still being done. It is the oldest and most effective answer to plain preaching: not to refute it but to assign it a tone, so that any man who speaks directly about sin can be dismissed as canting. The device requires no argument and is therefore always available.

The principle to recover is that the prophet's plainness is a gift of the Spirit and not a temperament, and that its content is specified: “to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin” (Mic 3:8). Jeremiah records what it costs to keep silent instead: “But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jer 20:9).

“they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13) — the plainness that was mistaken for cant.

pos: n. (John Menzies, 1624–1684, Aberdeen professor of divinity, who changed sides repeatedly)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; Menzies, a Scottish form of the Norman Mesnieres, pronounced Mingies.
biblical_def: John Menzies was professor of divinity at Marischal College, Aberdeen, for most of the years between 1649 and his death, and his career is the clearest instance in Scottish church history of a learned man who could not stay in one position. He began as a Protester and an Independent in sympathy, conformed to the episcopal establishment at the Restoration and held his chair under it, subscribed the declaration against the Covenant, then protested in the 1670s against aspects of the settlement he had subscribed, then conformed again. He was genuinely able: his disputations against the Jesuit Dempster and the Quakers were respected, and he trained many ministers. He was also, as his own contemporaries said without malice and with regret, a man whose convictions moved with the times, and no party could rely on him for a decade together. The dictionary records him because the corpus needs the honest negative instance as much as the exemplary one. “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jam 1:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines double-minded as having different minds at different times, unsettled, and stedfast as fixed, firm, constant.
webster_full: DOU'BLE-MINDED, a. Having different minds at different times; unsettled; wavering; unstable.
STED'FAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; firmly adhering to; constant; resolute.
LUKE'WARM, a. Moderately warm; indifferent; not ardent; not zealous.
SUBSCRI'BE, v. To assent to; to attest by writing one's name beneath.
scriptures: Jam 1:8
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
Hos 6:4
O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee? for your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away.
For their heart was not right with him, neither were they stedfast in his covenant.
Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
corruption_summary: The Aberdeen professor whose convictions moved with the government.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern treatment of a man like Menzies is to praise him: here, it is said, was a flexible mind, free of party spirit, willing to revise, a welcome contrast to the rigid men around him. Revision on evidence is a virtue. What Menzies did was something else, and his contemporaries on every side noticed it — his revisions tracked the government of the day with a regularity that evidence does not have.

The principle to recover is that stability is itself a Christian duty and instability a named fault: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jam 1:8). The psalmist diagnoses the root beneath the behaviour, which is not intellectual but covenantal: “For their heart was not right with him, neither were they stedfast in his covenant” (Psa 78:37). Hosea supplies the figure: a goodness that goes off like a morning cloud.

Greek akatastatos (G182) — unstable, unsettled, restless; James 1:8.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — kindness, goodness, covenant love; Hosea 6:4.

usage: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jam 1:8) — four changes of side in thirty years.
“your goodness is as a morning cloud” (Hos 6:4) — what his parties learned to expect.
“neither were they stedfast in his covenant” (Psa 78:37) — the root beneath the record.

pos: n. (James Sharp, 1618–1679, Resolutioner envoy who became Archbishop of St Andrews and chief persecutor of the Covenanters)
etymology: Hebrew Yaaqob, he takes by the heel, through Latin Jacobus and Spanish Iago to James; Sharp, keen, from Old English scearp.
biblical_def: James Sharp was minister of Crail and one of the abler young men of the Resolutioner party, and in 1660 that party sent him to London as its agent, trusted to secure the Presbyterian settlement of the Church of Scotland from the restored king. He wrote home reassuringly for months while negotiating otherwise, accepted episcopacy, and in December 1661 was consecrated Archbishop of St Andrews and primate of Scotland. From that seat he was the principal author of the policy that ejected some four hundred ministers, outlawed field preaching, quartered troops on the west, and set up the High Commission; he pressed the prosecution of James Guthrie to the scaffold, a man who had been his colleague. In May 1679 a party of nine Covenanters, finding him on the road, dragged him from his coach on Magus Muir before his daughter and killed him. The dictionary names the betrayal as betrayal and the killing as murder; the one does not justify the other. “But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance” (Psa 55:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to betray as to disclose or deliver up treacherously, and vengeance as the infliction of pain in return for an injury.
webster_full: BETRA'Y, v. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud; to violate by fraud.
VEN'GEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offence; retribution.
PRI'MATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in a national church; an archbishop.
INTEG'RITY, n. Uprightness; honesty; probity; entire correspondence with the rule of right.
scriptures: But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.
Pro 11:3
The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: The envoy who sold the settlement he was sent to secure, and was murdered on Magus Muir.
corruption_paragraphs: Sharp is handled badly from two directions. Episcopalian writers have presented him as a realist who saw that Presbytery was not obtainable and did his best within the possible, which the surviving letters do not permit: he was writing one thing to Edinburgh and doing another in London. And a strand of Covenanting apology has treated his killing as an execution of justice by men acting on the Covenant's authority, which the dictionary refuses outright. Nine men with swords on a public road are not a court.

The principle to recover is that vengeance is reserved and that its reservation is not a weakness in the cause of the oppressed but the ground of their hope: “avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). And the sowing is not escaped either way: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7).

Hebrew tummah (H8538) — integrity, uprightness; Proverbs 11:3.
Greek mukterizo (G3456) — to turn up the nose at, mock; Galatians 6:7.
Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — vengeance, retribution; Romans 12:19.
usage: “a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance” (Psa 55:13) — the colleague he sent to the scaffold.
“The integrity of the upright shall guide them” (Pro 11:3) — the letters from London of 1660.
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19) — against Magus Muir, 1679.

pos: n. (Alexander Craighead, 1707–1766, Covenanter minister in Pennsylvania, Virginia and North Carolina)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; Craighead, the head of the crag, a Scottish place-name.
biblical_def: Alexander Craighead carried the Scottish Covenanting tradition into the American colonies. Son of an Ulster-Scots minister, licensed in Pennsylvania, he sided with the New Side in the Great Awakening and was censured for irregular preaching; then he went further, and in November 1743 at Middle Octorara he gathered a company who publicly renewed the National Covenant and the Solemn League and Covenant, with drawn swords, and published the proceedings. The Synod of Philadelphia suspended him; he ministered to the Covenanter societies, moved to the Virginia frontier, and from 1758 was the first settled pastor in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, serving seven congregations in the Catawba valley until his death. The covenanting doctrine he preached there — that a people may bind themselves by oath to God against a government that breaks his law — was still being quoted in Mecklenburg a decade later, and the connection with the resistance that followed has long been remarked. “And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul” (2Ch 15:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual consent or agreement, and to renew as to make new again, to repeat.
webster_full: COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons to do or forbear some act.
RENEW', v. To renovate; to restore to a former state; to repeat; to begin again.
SO'CIETY, n. A number of persons united for a common interest; in Scotland, a praying society of Covenanters.
FRON'TIER, n. The marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country.
scriptures: And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;

And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.
So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem.
Jer 50:5
They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten.
corruption_summary: The Covenanter of the Catawba, who renewed the Covenants at Middle Octorara with drawn swords.
corruption_paragraphs: Craighead is now claimed chiefly as a political ancestor — the preacher who seeded the Mecklenburg resistance — and the claim is made so eagerly that the covenanting theology underneath it disappears. He did not teach a doctrine of natural rights. He taught that a nation stands under oath to God, that its rulers are bound by the same oath, and that the people may testify against rulers who break it. The political consequence was real and was a consequence, not the thing itself.

The principle to recover is that public covenanting is a biblical act with biblical precedent, performed by a people and not merely by individuals: “And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3). The renewal of such an oath after a generation's neglect is exactly what Asa's Judah did — “And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul” (2Ch 15:12) — and what Craighead's company did at Middle Octorara in 1743.

Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, inquire, require; 2 Chronicles 15:12.
Hebrew amad (H5975) — to stand, take one's stand; 2 Kings 23:3.
Hebrew karath (H3772) — to cut, to cut a covenant; Joshua 24:25.
Hebrew olam (H5769) — everlasting, perpetual; Jeremiah 50:5.

“And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3) — public covenanting as a biblical act.
